html:
Afro-Costa Ricans are mostly descendants of Jamaican and other West Indian workers who came to the Caribbean coast of Costa Rica from 1872 to build the railway and work on banana plantations.

They settled around the port of Limón, spoke English, and many were Protestant, unlike the Spanish-speaking Catholic Central Valley. When the United Fruit Company left the coast in the 1930s, they were barred by law from taking jobs on its new Pacific plantations and few could move inland. Most were denied citizenship.

The constitution of 1949 made them full citizens, after the civil war and under José Figueres. Limón keeps its own food, calypso music and English Creole. Their story ties Costa Rica to the wider Caribbean of migrant workers.
sum: Afro-Costa Ricans are mostly descendants of Jamaican and other West Indian workers who came to the Caribbean coast of Costa Rica from 1872 to build the railway and work on banana plantations.
